intro: A text does not explain itself. Readers explain it, and they do so from their own place and time. This unit follows Buddhist readers across two thousand years, from a monk answering a Greek king about a chariot to a Dalit leader in 1956 and a Vietnamese monk writing about a cloud in a sheet of paper.

The first chapter traces the teaching of not-self through the classical thinkers: the Pali suttas and the Questions of King Milinda, Buddhaghosa, Nagarjuna and the doctrine of emptiness, Yogacara, and the schools of Tibet and China. The second follows modern readers: reformers, engaged Buddhists, converts and heritage communities, scientists, women seeking ordination and environmentalists.

By the end you will be able to explain how one term, such as not-self, has been read in several ways; describe modern movements accurately and without ranking them; and analyze any reading by asking which passages it cites, what question it answers and which community it speaks for.
bigQuestion: Why do faithful readers of the same Buddhist texts reach such different understandings, and how can a student describe them fairly?

title: Interpreters Across the Centuries

chapters.title: Not-Self and Emptiness: Classical Readers
chapters.bigQuestion: How did Buddhist thinkers across Asia read the teaching of not-self, and why did they reach such different accounts of it?

story.title: What Is a Chariot?
story.kicker: A Greek king asks a monk his name, and the monk answers with a question about the king's own chariot.
paragraphs: The Questions of King Milinda opens with a meeting that Buddhists have retold for two thousand years. King Milinda, whom scholars identify with the Indo-Greek ruler Menander, who reigned in the second century BCE, comes to meet a monk named Nagasena. The king asks the obvious first question: what is your name?

Nagasena answers that he is called Nagasena, but that this is only a name, a way of speaking. No permanent person is found here, he says. The king pounces. If there is no person, who wears the robe, who eats the food, who keeps the precepts? If someone killed you, would there be no killer? Is Nagasena the hair? The teeth? The feelings? Nagasena says no to each.

Then Nagasena turns the questions around. Did the king come on foot or by chariot? By chariot. Then what is the chariot? Is it the pole? The axle? The wheels? The frame? No, the king says to each. Is it something apart from them all? No again. Then, says Nagasena, where is this chariot you rode?

The king sees the point. Chariot, he says, is the name used when the parts are put together. Just so, says Nagasena, Nagasena is the name used for the parts of a person. This chapter follows that idea, not-self, through the great classical readers of Asia, from the Pali commentators to Nagarjuna, Yogacara and the schools of Tibet and China.
story.think: Does Nagasena's answer mean the chariot, or Nagasena, is unreal? What exactly has he denied?

lessons.title: The Discourse on Not-Self
lessons.mainIdea: The Anattalakkhana Sutta argues that none of the five aggregates can be a self, because each is impermanent and not under full control.
reading: Pali tradition places the Anattalakkhana Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 22.59, just after the first sermon, spoken to the same five monks. It takes the five *aggregates* one by one: form, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness. Each, the sutta says, is not self. Its argument has two steps.

First, if form were self, it would not lead to affliction, and one could say, let my form be thus. But one cannot command it. The same holds for the other four. Second, the Buddha, as the sutta presents him, asks whether each aggregate is permanent or impermanent. Impermanent, the monks answer. Is what is impermanent suffering or ease? Suffering. Is it fit to regard what is impermanent and suffering as 'this is mine, this I am, this is my self'? No.

The sutta ends with the five monks reaching awakening. Scholars note what it does and does not claim. It denies that any aggregate is a self. It does not, in so many words, state that there is no self anywhere. That gap is where later readers split. The key term is *anatta*, not-self, which the sutta joins with impermanence and suffering as three marks of existence.

words.d: not-self; Sanskrit anatman: the teaching that no aggregate is a lasting self
khandha/skandha: form, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness
impermanence, suffering and not-self, which Buddhist texts say mark all conditioned things
Samyutta Nikaya 22.59, the discourse on the characteristic of not-self

look.title: Is This Mine?
look.text: The Buddha asks whether form is permanent or impermanent. The monks say impermanent. Is what is impermanent suffering or ease? Suffering. Then is it fit to regard it as 'this is mine, this I am, this is my self'? No, venerable sir.
look.cite: Anattalakkhana Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 22.59; paraphrased (cf. tr. Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Connected Discourses of the Buddha, 2000)
look.prompt: Rebuild the argument in three premises and a conclusion. Which premise does the most work?

check.q: What are the five aggregates?
check.why: SN 22.59 examines these five khandhas.

check.q: What does SN 22.59 explicitly deny, as scholars read it?
choices: That any aggregate is a self
check.why: The sutta denies that each aggregate is self; whether it denies any self at all is debated.

check.q: Which three marks does Buddhist teaching join together?
check.why: Anicca, dukkha and anatta are the three marks.

lessons.title: The Chariot and the Name
lessons.mainIdea: The Questions of King Milinda uses the chariot simile to argue that 'person' is a name for a set of parts, not a hidden self.
reading: The Milindapanha, or Questions of King Milinda, is a Pali dialogue probably compiled over several centuries around the turn of the common era. Theravada tradition treats it with great respect, and in Myanmar it is included in the Khuddaka Nikaya. Rhys Davids translated it in 1890 and 1894. Its most famous passage is the *chariot simile*.

The argument works by analysis. Take a chariot apart and no single part is the chariot. Nor is the chariot something extra beyond the parts. Yet the word chariot is useful and correct in daily speech. Nagasena draws the parallel: a person is a convention, a name for aggregates put together, while no self is found among or beyond them.

The simile has an earlier source. In Samyutta Nikaya 5.10, the nun Vajira uses the chariot image to answer Mara, the tempter. Just as the word chariot is used when parts are assembled, she says, so being is used when the aggregates are present. So the Milindapanha builds on a line credited to a woman teacher in the canon. Scholars see it as a clear early statement of *conventional* designation.

words.d: the Questions of King Milinda: a Pali dialogue between King Milinda and the monk Nagasena
the argument that 'chariot' and 'person' are names for assembled parts
agreed on for everyday use; a conventional name is useful but does not point to a hidden essence
a Buddhist nun who, in SN 5.10, uses the chariot image to answer Mara

look.title: The Nun Vajira's Answer
look.text: Vajira tells Mara that just as the word 'chariot' is used when the parts are assembled, so the word 'being' is used when the aggregates are present. There is only suffering arising and passing, she says; no being is found.
look.cite: Vajira Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 5.10; paraphrased (cf. tr. Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Connected Discourses of the Buddha, 2000)
look.prompt: Compare Vajira's lines with Nagasena's. What does the later dialogue add?

check.q: Whom do scholars identify King Milinda with?
check.why: Milinda is commonly identified with Menander, second century BCE.

check.q: Who uses the chariot image earlier, in SN 5.10?
check.why: Vajira answers Mara with the chariot image.

check.q: What does the chariot simile claim about a person?
choices: 'Person' is a name for assembled aggregates, with no self found among or beyond them
The self lives in the axle
check.why: The simile treats 'person' as a conventional designation.

lessons.title: Who Is Reborn?
lessons.mainIdea: Not-self raised the question of what continues in rebirth, and Nagasena answers with the image of a flame passed from lamp to lamp.
reading: If there is no lasting self, readers have long asked, who is reborn and who receives the results of karma? King Milinda presses this. Nagasena answers that the one reborn is neither the same person nor a different one. He gives an image: a lamp lit from another lamp. Is the flame the same? Not exactly. Is it unrelated? No. It depends on the first.

The same holds, Nagasena says, for a child and the old man it becomes, or milk that turns to curd and then to butter. There is *continuity* by causes, not identity of a substance. Theravada teachers use this reasoning to hold both karma and not-self: actions shape later states, but no unchanging owner carries them.

Not all early Buddhists accepted this answer. A group called the Pudgalavadins, or Personalists, held that a person (pudgala) is real, neither the same as nor different from the aggregates. Other schools, including the Theravada in the Kathavatthu, argued against them. The debate shows that not-self was contested from within Buddhism, not only from outside it.

words.d: a chain of connected states where each depends on the one before
an early Buddhist school that held the 'person' to be real in a special sense
Points of Controversy: a Theravada Abhidhamma text that argues against rival Buddhist views

look.title: Lamp to Lamp
look.text: Nagasena: a man lights a second lamp from the first. The flame in the second is not the flame in the first, yet it did not come from nowhere. So, he says, is rebirth: neither the same nor another.
look.prompt: Does the lamp image solve the puzzle of karma without a self, or restate it? Argue one side from the image's details.

check.q: How does Nagasena describe the one who is reborn?
choices: Neither the same nor a different person
check.why: His lamp image expresses 'neither the same nor another.'

check.q: What did the Pudgalavadins hold?
choices: The person is real, neither the same as nor different from the aggregates
check.why: The Personalists affirmed a real pudgala in a special sense.

check.q: What does the Pudgalavada debate show?
check.why: Rival Buddhist schools argued over the person.

lessons.title: Buddhaghosa's Path of Purification
lessons.mainIdea: In the fifth century CE, Buddhaghosa's Visuddhimagga set out a systematic Theravada account of practice and of the person as a flow of states.
reading: Buddhaghosa came to Sri Lanka from India in the fifth century CE, tradition says, and worked at the Mahavihara monastery in Anuradhapura. He wrote or edited many Pali commentaries and one great summary, the *Visuddhimagga*, the Path of Purification. It organizes the path into virtue, concentration and wisdom, following a verse in the Samyutta Nikaya.

On not-self, Buddhaghosa is systematic. A person is analyzed into mind and matter, nama-rupa, and further into momentary states that arise and cease in dependence on conditions. He quotes a line many teachers repeat: there is suffering, but no sufferer; there is doing, but no doer; there is a path, but no one who travels it. This is not-self stated as a method of seeing.

For most of Theravada history, Buddhaghosa's reading has been the standard one. Monks in Sri Lanka, Myanmar and Thailand learn the texts through his commentaries. Some modern teachers, especially in Thai forest traditions, have questioned parts of his system and returned to the suttas directly. The Visuddhimagga remains a central *commentarial* voice.

words.d: the Path of Purification: Buddhaghosa's fifth-century summary of Theravada teaching
mind and matter; the two sides into which Pali analysis divides a person
belonging to the commentaries, the later texts that explain the canon
the Great Monastery at Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka, center of Theravada orthodoxy

look.title: No Doer, Only Doing
look.text: Buddhaghosa quotes the ancients: there is suffering but no one who suffers; there is doing but no doer; there is extinction but no one extinguished; there is a path but no traveler on it.
look.cite: Buddhaghosa, Visuddhimagga 16.90; paraphrased (cf. tr. Bhikkhu Nanamoli, The Path of Purification, 1956)
look.prompt: How is this line an application of the chariot simile? Explain in two sentences.

check.q: Where did Buddhaghosa work, as tradition says?
choices: The Mahavihara in Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka
check.why: Tradition places him at the Mahavihara in the fifth century CE.

check.q: What are the three parts of the path in the Visuddhimagga?
check.why: The book is organized as sila, samadhi and panna.

check.q: How have some Thai forest teachers related to Buddhaghosa?
choices: They questioned parts of his system and returned to the suttas
check.why: Some forest teachers emphasized the suttas over the commentaries.

lessons.title: Abhidhamma: A List of Moments
lessons.mainIdea: The Abhidhamma analyzes experience into momentary events called dhammas, a method that later Mahayana critics would question.
reading: The *Abhidhamma*, the third basket of the Pali Canon, restates the teaching as analysis. It lists the basic events, called dhammas, that make up experience: kinds of consciousness, mental factors, material qualities and nibbana. Theravada lists 89 or 121 types of consciousness and 52 mental factors.

In this picture, a person is a rapid stream of dhammas, each lasting a moment. Not-self follows: examine the stream and find only events, no owner. Other early schools built their own Abhidharma systems. The Sarvastivada school, strong in northwest India, held that dhammas exist in past, present and future, which is what its name means.

The method was powerful, but it raised a question. If the self is empty because it breaks down into dhammas, are the dhammas themselves real? The Abhidhamma schools said each dhamma has its own nature, *svabhava* in Sanskrit. The Mahayana philosopher Nagarjuna would argue that even dhammas lack such a nature. That argument is the subject of the next section.

words.d: the third basket of the Pali Canon, which analyzes experience into basic events; Abhidharma in Sanskrit
in Abhidhamma, a basic momentary event or element of experience
own-nature: the idea that a thing has its own independent essence
an early school that held dhammas exist in past, present and future

look.title: Theravada Abhidhamma Categories
look.cite: Abhidhammattha Sangaha, ed. and tr. Bhikkhu Bodhi, A Comprehensive Manual of Abhidhamma (1993)
look.prompt: Why might a system that lists every kind of mental event still claim to find no self?

check.q: What is a dhamma in Abhidhamma analysis?
choices: A basic momentary event of experience
check.why: The Abhidhamma analyzes experience into dhammas.

check.q: What did the Sarvastivada school hold?
choices: Dhammas exist in past, present and future
check.why: Sarvastivada means 'the doctrine that all exists.'

check.q: What does svabhava mean?
check.why: Svabhava is the idea of a thing's own independent nature.

lessons.title: Emptiness of Everything
lessons.mainIdea: Nagarjuna, c. second century CE, argued that all things, including the dhammas, are empty of own-nature because they arise dependently.
reading: *Nagarjuna* lived in South India, probably in the second century CE, though his dates are uncertain. Mahayana Buddhists in Tibet and East Asia honor him as a second Buddha. His main work is the Mulamadhyamakakarika, the Root Verses on the Middle Way, in 27 chapters. The school built on it is called Madhyamaka, the Middle.

His central claim is that all things are empty, *shunya*, of svabhava. A thing that had its own-nature would not depend on anything and would not change. But everything arises in dependence on causes and parts. So nothing has own-nature. In the famous verse 24.18, as usually read, he says that dependent arising is what he calls emptiness, and that this is itself the middle way.

Nagarjuna thus pushed not-self further. The Abhidhamma had said the person is empty because it is made of dhammas. Nagarjuna said the dhammas are empty too. Madhyamaka thinkers stress that emptiness is not nothingness. It is the absence of independent essence. Critics in other schools, Buddhist and Hindu, argued that the view slid toward nihilism, a charge Madhyamaka writers answered at length.

words.d: an Indian Buddhist philosopher, c. second century CE, founder of the Madhyamaka school
emptiness: in Madhyamaka, the lack of independent own-nature in all things
pratityasamutpada: the teaching that things arise in dependence on conditions
the Middle Way school based on Nagarjuna's works

look.title: Root Verses 24.18
look.text: Nagarjuna says that whatever arises dependently is what is called emptiness; that emptiness is a dependent designation, and it is the middle way.
look.cite: Nagarjuna, Mulamadhyamakakarika 24.18; paraphrased (cf. tr. Jay L. Garfield, The Fundamental Wisdom of the Middle Way, 1995)
look.prompt: Why does the verse call emptiness itself a 'dependent designation'? What would it mean if emptiness were a thing with its own nature?

check.q: What is Nagarjuna's main work?
choices: Mulamadhyamakakarika, Root Verses on the Middle Way
check.why: The Root Verses are the base text of Madhyamaka.

check.q: According to Madhyamaka, what are things empty of?
check.why: Emptiness is the lack of svabhava, not nothingness.

check.q: How did Nagarjuna extend the Abhidhamma analysis?
choices: He said the dhammas themselves are empty
He said the self is permanent
check.why: Nagarjuna argued even dhammas lack own-nature.

lessons.title: Two Truths
lessons.mainIdea: Nagarjuna distinguishes conventional truth from ultimate truth and says the ultimate is taught only through the conventional.
reading: In the Root Verses 24.8 to 24.10, Nagarjuna says the Buddhas teach by means of *two truths*: a conventional truth and an ultimate truth. Those who do not understand the difference, he says, do not understand the deep point of the teaching. And without relying on the conventional, the ultimate cannot be taught.

Conventional truth is how things appear and are named in ordinary life: chariots, persons, cause and effect. Ultimate truth, for Madhyamaka, is their emptiness. The two are not two worlds. They are two ways of seeing the same things. This lets Madhyamaka affirm ethics, karma and practice at the conventional level while denying own-nature at the ultimate.

Readers connect the two truths to the chariot simile and to verse 160 of the Dhammapada. Many later schools adopted the distinction but drew its line in different places. Some Tibetan schools debated whether the ultimate can be stated in words at all. The concept became one of the most widely used tools in Buddhist *hermeneutics*, the art of interpreting texts.

words.d: conventional truth and ultimate truth, two levels on which Buddhist teachers say things are described
paramartha: in Madhyamaka, the emptiness of all things
the theory and method of interpreting texts

look.title: Two Truths at Work
look.text: Conventional: Maya read verse 160 and asked a question. Ultimate, for Madhyamaka: 'Maya', 'verse' and 'question' are empty of own-nature, dependently arisen. Madhyamaka writers say the second statement does not cancel the first.
look.prompt: How could a Madhyamaka reader keep ethics meaningful if persons are ultimately empty? Use the two truths.

check.q: Where does Nagarjuna set out the two truths?
check.why: MMK 24.8-10 names conventional and ultimate truth.

check.q: What is ultimate truth for Madhyamaka?
check.why: For Madhyamaka, emptiness is the ultimate truth.

check.q: What does hermeneutics mean?
choices: The theory and method of interpreting texts
check.why: Hermeneutics is the art of interpretation.

lessons.title: Yogacara: Mind Only
lessons.mainIdea: The Yogacara school of Asanga and Vasubandhu, c. fourth century CE, analyzed experience as the work of consciousness.
reading: *Yogacara*, the practice-of-yoga school, arose in India around the fourth century CE. Tradition names two brothers, Asanga and Vasubandhu, as its founders. It is also called Vijnanavada, the way of consciousness, or cittamatra, mind only. Its texts include the Samdhinirmocana Sutra and Vasubandhu's Twenty Verses and Thirty Verses.

Yogacara analyzes experience as the work of consciousness. It describes eight kinds, including a storehouse consciousness, alaya-vijnana, where the seeds of past actions are kept until they ripen. This offered an account of karma and continuity without a self: a stream of seeds, not an owner.

Scholars debate what mind only means. Some read Yogacara as idealism: only mind exists. Others read it as a method of practice: attend to how experience is constructed, and set aside questions about what lies beyond it. Tibetan scholars, East Asian schools such as Faxiang, and modern Western philosophers have all argued over the reading. Madhyamaka critics said Yogacara made consciousness too real.

words.d: a Mahayana school, c. fourth century CE, that analyzes experience as the work of consciousness
storehouse consciousness: in Yogacara, the store of seeds from past actions
the philosophical view that reality is mental or mind-dependent
an Indian Buddhist philosopher, c. fourth century CE, author of key Yogacara verse texts

look.title: Two Readings of 'Mind Only'
look.text: Reading 1: only consciousness exists; there are no outer objects. Reading 2: study how consciousness builds the world we meet, and do not claim to know more. Both readings cite Vasubandhu's Twenty Verses.
look.prompt: Which reading would a practitioner and which would a metaphysician be more drawn to? Explain.

check.q: Who are named as founders of Yogacara?
check.why: Tradition names the brothers Asanga and Vasubandhu.

check.q: What is the alaya-vijnana?
choices: A storehouse consciousness holding seeds of past actions
check.why: Yogacara describes it as the store of karmic seeds.

check.q: What did Madhyamaka critics say about Yogacara?
check.why: Madhyamaka thinkers held that consciousness too is empty.

lessons.title: Tibet: Debating Emptiness
lessons.mainIdea: Tibetan scholastic schools made Madhyamaka central and debated how emptiness should be understood, most famously in Tsongkhapa's Gelug tradition.
reading: Buddhism in Tibet drew heavily on the Indian monastic universities, such as Nalanda. Tibetan scholars translated Indian texts into Tibetan and organized study around them. Madhyamaka came to be regarded by most Tibetan schools as the highest philosophical view. Monks still learn it through formal *debate*, with clapping and questions in the monastery courtyard.

Tsongkhapa (1357 to 1419), founder of the Gelug school to which the Dalai Lamas belong, argued that emptiness must be understood precisely. What is negated is inherent existence, he said, not conventional existence. Other Tibetan thinkers read emptiness differently. Some in the Jonang school held an 'other-emptiness' view: the ultimate is empty of what is other than it, but not empty of itself.

These debates were serious and sometimes sharp. Tibetan traditions also held that intellectual understanding must be joined to practice. A careful student notes that Tibetan readers share the texts and many terms but drew different conclusions, and each school claims fidelity to Nagarjuna.

words.d: in Tibetan monasteries, a formal practice of question and answer used to study philosophy
Tibetan scholar (1357-1419), founder of the Gelug school
a Tibetan Buddhist school founded by Tsongkhapa, to which the Dalai Lamas belong
shentong: a Tibetan view that the ultimate is empty of what is other than itself

look.title: What Is Negated?
look.text: Tsongkhapa: the chariot exists conventionally; what does not exist is a chariot with its own inherent nature. A Jonang teacher: the ultimate is empty of passing, conventional things, but its own nature is not empty.
look.prompt: State in one sentence what each view says is 'empty of' what.

check.q: Which school did Tsongkhapa found?
check.why: Tsongkhapa founded the Gelug school.

check.q: According to Tsongkhapa, what does emptiness negate?
check.why: He stressed a precise object of negation.

check.q: How do Tibetan monks commonly study Madhyamaka?
check.why: Courtyard debate is a hallmark of Tibetan monastic study.

lessons.title: China: Harmony and Interpenetration
lessons.mainIdea: Chinese schools such as Tiantai and Huayan read emptiness in terms of harmony and the interpenetration of all things.
reading: When Indian texts reached China, readers interpreted them through new questions and a new language. Zhiyi (538 to 597), founder of the Tiantai school, taught three truths: emptiness, conventional existence, and the middle that holds both. He organized the sutras into a sequence, with the Lotus Sutra at the summit.

The Huayan school, systematized by Fazang (643 to 712), drew on the Avatamsaka Sutra. It taught the *interpenetration* of all things: each phenomenon contains and reflects every other. Fazang is said to have explained this to Empress Wu with a golden lion statue, and later writers used the image of Indra's net, in which each jewel reflects all the others.

These readings keep emptiness and dependent arising but give them a warmer, more cosmic tone. Scholars note that Chinese ideas about harmony may have shaped them. Chan, later Zen, drew on these schools while stressing direct experience over doctrine. The same Indian terms, read in China, opened new *interpretations* without leaving the tradition.

words.d: a Chinese Buddhist school founded by Zhiyi, known for the three truths and for honoring the Lotus Sutra
a Chinese school based on the Avatamsaka Sutra that taught the interpenetration of all things
the idea that every thing contains and reflects every other
a reader's account of what a text means

look.title: Indra's Net
look.text: Huayan writers describe a net hung in the palace of Indra, with a jewel at every knot. Each jewel reflects every other jewel, and each reflection holds the reflections of all the rest.
look.cite: Image drawn from the Avatamsaka Sutra tradition as developed by Fazang and Dushun; paraphrased (cf. Francis H. Cook, Hua-yen Buddhism: The Jewel Net of Indra, 1977)
look.prompt: How does this image extend Nagarjuna's dependent arising? What does it add?

check.q: What did Zhiyi teach?
choices: Three truths: emptiness, conventional existence and the middle
check.why: Zhiyi's Tiantai school taught the threefold truth.

check.q: Which sutra is the basis of the Huayan school?
check.why: Huayan is named after the Avatamsaka (Huayan) Sutra.

check.q: What does Indra's net illustrate?
check.why: Each jewel reflects all the others.

review.q: What does SN 22.59 examine to show not-self?
review.why: The Anattalakkhana Sutta takes each aggregate in turn.

chapters.title: Modern Readers: Engaged, Reform and Convert Buddhism
chapters.bigQuestion: How have modern readers, inside and outside Asia, reread the Buddhist texts to meet new questions of justice, science and equality?

story.title: The Refuges at Nagpur
story.kicker: On one October day in 1956, a huge crowd in central India repeats three short lines after a lawyer and statesman.
paragraphs: On October 14, 1956, an open ground in the city of Nagpur fills with people dressed in white. Estimates of the crowd vary, but most accounts say hundreds of thousands came. Most belong to communities then called untouchable, now often called Dalit. They have come to hear Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.

Ambedkar is one of the best-known people in India. Born into a Dalit family in 1891, he earned doctorates from Columbia University and the London School of Economics. He chaired the committee that drafted India's Constitution. For decades he fought caste discrimination. In 1935 he had said he was born a Hindu but would not die one.

That morning, Ambedkar and his wife take the Three Refuges and Five Precepts from the senior monk Chandramani. Then Ambedkar turns to the crowd and leads them in the refuges, the precepts and twenty-two vows of his own composition. The crowd repeats each line. In a few hours, one of the largest mass conversions in modern history has taken place.

Ambedkar died less than two months later. His book The Buddha and His Dhamma, published in 1957, reread the Buddhist texts as a charter of social equality. This chapter looks at Ambedkar and other modern readers: reformers, engaged Buddhists, scientists, women seeking ordination and environmentalists. Each reads old texts in a new light.
story.think: Why might a social reformer choose an ancient religious text as the ground for a movement for equality?

lessons.title: What Modernism Means
lessons.mainIdea: Scholars use 'Buddhist modernism' for movements since the 1800s that present Buddhism as rational, ethical and compatible with science.
reading: From the late 1800s, Asian and Western Buddhists began presenting their tradition in new ways. Colonial rule, Christian missions, printing and science all put pressure on older forms. Reformers answered by stressing meditation, ethics and reason, and by downplaying ritual, gods and miracles. Scholars call this broad pattern *Buddhist modernism*.

David McMahan's The Making of Buddhist Modernism (2008) traces its sources: European ideas about science and individual experience, Romantic ideas about nature and the self, and Asian reform movements. In Sri Lanka, Anagarika Dharmapala (1864 to 1933) led a Buddhist revival. He spoke at the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago in 1893, as did the Japanese Zen teacher Soyen Shaku.

Modernism is not one school. It runs through Theravada, Zen and Tibetan communities alike. Some scholars and traditional Buddhists caution that modernist readings can lose the devotion, ritual and cosmology that many Asian Buddhists hold central. Others see modernism as one more chapter in a long history of *adaptation*. Most scholars describe it rather than judge it.

words.d: movements since the 1800s that present Buddhism as rational, ethical and compatible with science
change that fits a tradition to a new time or place
a movement to renew a tradition's strength and practice
Sri Lankan Buddhist reformer (1864-1933) who spoke in Chicago in 1893

lessons.title: Ambedkar's Buddhism
lessons.mainIdea: Ambedkar reread the Buddhist texts as a teaching of social equality, and his movement is today called Navayana by many followers.
reading: In The Buddha and His Dhamma (1957), Ambedkar retold the Buddha's life and teaching. He rejected parts of the tradition that he felt did not fit reason or justice. He questioned the traditional account of the Four Sights. He read suffering as including social suffering from poverty and caste. He stressed that the Buddha, as the texts present him, admitted people of every caste to the *sangha*.

His twenty-two vows set out a break with Hindu practice and a commitment to equality, reason and the precepts. Many of his followers call their tradition *Navayana*, the new vehicle, though the name is not used by all. They honor Ambedkar as Babasaheb and gather each year at Nagpur on the anniversary of the conversion.

Other Buddhists have responded in several ways. Some traditional scholars say Ambedkar departed from the texts on karma and rebirth. Many Dalit Buddhists see his work as recovering the texts' true social core. Scholars such as Christopher Queen treat his movement as a major example of socially engaged Buddhism. In India today, most Buddhists belong to communities shaped by his conversion.

words.d: the new vehicle: a name many followers use for Ambedkar's Buddhism
the name many people formerly called untouchable use for themselves in India
a hereditary social rank in South Asia
the community of monks and nuns, or of all Buddhists

lessons.title: Converts and Heritage Communities
lessons.mainIdea: In the United States, Asian heritage Buddhist communities and convert communities read and practice the texts in overlapping but different ways.
reading: American Buddhism is diverse. Many Buddhists in the United States belong to Asian heritage communities: Japanese, Chinese, Vietnamese, Thai, Lao, Cambodian, Korean, Sri Lankan, Tibetan and more. The Buddhist Temple of Chicago, founded in 1944 by Rev. Gyomay Kubose, grew from a Japanese American Jodo Shinshu community after World War II.

Other American Buddhists are *converts*, people who came to Buddhism as adults, often through meditation centers, books or Zen and Tibetan teachers. Convert communities often stress meditation and read texts like the Satipatthana Sutta or the Heart Sutra closely. Heritage temples often center family ritual, festivals, chanting for the dead and language classes for children.

Scholars once described these as two Buddhisms, but many now call that too simple. Heritage communities include meditators; convert communities include ritual; children of immigrants and converts share centers. Some Asian American Buddhists have written about being overlooked when media present Buddhism as a white convert practice. A careful reader treats every community as an equal *interpreter* of the tradition.

words.d: a person who takes up a religion as an adult, not by birth
a religious community rooted in a family or cultural tradition passed down over generations
one who explains or lives out a text's meaning
True Pure Land Buddhism, a Japanese school centered on Amida Buddha

lessons.title: Thich Nhat Hanh and Interbeing
lessons.mainIdea: Thich Nhat Hanh coined or popularized 'engaged Buddhism' during the Vietnam War, reading the texts as a call to act for peace.
reading: Thich Nhat Hanh (1926 to 2022) was a Vietnamese Zen monk. During the Vietnam War he worked for peace, trained young volunteers in relief work, and in 1966 founded the Order of Interbeing. He used the phrase *engaged Buddhism* for practice that responds to suffering in society, not only within the self. His 1967 book Vietnam: Lotus in a Sea of Fire made the case in English.

He read classic texts through this lens. His word interbeing, drawn from Huayan teaching, says that nothing exists by itself; a sheet of paper contains the cloud, the rain and the logger. His Five Mindfulness Trainings restate the five precepts in positive, social terms: protecting life, practicing generosity, responsible sexual conduct, loving speech and mindful consumption.

Martin Luther King Jr. nominated him for the Nobel Peace Prize in 1967. Exiled from Vietnam for decades, he built Plum Village in France, which drew practitioners from many countries. Some traditional critics said he changed the precepts too freely; his students answer that he kept their spirit. He remains one of the most read modern Buddhist teachers.

words.d: Buddhist practice that responds to social and political suffering
Thich Nhat Hanh's word for the dependence of every thing on every other thing
Thich Nhat Hanh's restatement of the five precepts in social terms

lessons.title: Saigon, 1963
lessons.mainIdea: The self-immolation of Thich Quang Duc in 1963, a protest against government policy toward Buddhists, drew a wide range of Buddhist and public responses.
reading: On June 11, 1963, the monk Thich Quang Duc sat down at a busy intersection in Saigon and set himself on fire. He was protesting the South Vietnamese government of Ngo Dinh Diem, which Buddhists said discriminated against them. Earlier that spring, government forces had fired on Buddhists in Hue during Vesak, killing several people.

A photograph by the journalist Malcolm Browne showed the monk sitting still in the flames. It spread around the world and put great pressure on the Diem government, which fell in a coup that November. Several other monks and nuns later died in the same way. The event is part of the history of *engaged Buddhism*, though it is not a model the tradition teaches.

Buddhists have responded in different ways. Thich Nhat Hanh, in a 1965 letter to Martin Luther King Jr., described the act as not suicide but an expression of will to be heard. Some Theravada and other teachers point to the precept against taking life and say they cannot approve. Many regard Thich Quang Duc with reverence. A careful student reports these views and the *context* without urging any view of the act.

words.d: setting oneself on fire, usually as a public protest
the events and conditions surrounding an act
Buddhist practice that responds to social and political suffering

lessons.title: The Dalai Lama and Science
lessons.mainIdea: The Fourteenth Dalai Lama has promoted dialogue with scientists and said Buddhist claims contradicted by science should be revised.
reading: Tenzin Gyatso, the Fourteenth *Dalai Lama*, was born in 1935 and has lived in exile in India since 1959. Tibetan Buddhists regard him as a manifestation of the bodhisattva of compassion, Avalokiteshvara. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989. Since 1987 he has met scientists in the Mind and Life dialogues on mind, meditation and the brain.

In The Universe in a Single Atom (2005), he wrote that if science proves a Buddhist claim wrong, Buddhists must accept the finding and give up the claim. He applied this to the traditional cosmology of a flat world with a central mountain, Meru, which he said can be set aside. He did not apply it to rebirth or consciousness, which he said science has not disproven.

His approach is a clear case of *modernist* reading from within a traditional lineage. Some scientists praise the dialogues as open inquiry. Some scholars ask whether meditation research strips practices from their religious setting. Some traditional Tibetan teachers keep the older cosmology in teaching. Each reader weighs text, lineage and evidence differently.

words.d: the title of a line of Tibetan teachers in the Gelug school; the Fourteenth is Tenzin Gyatso
the bodhisattva of compassion, whom Tibetan Buddhists believe the Dalai Lama embodies
belonging to Buddhist modernism: stressing reason, ethics and science
the central mountain of traditional Buddhist and Hindu cosmology

lessons.title: Nuns and Full Ordination
lessons.mainIdea: The Vinaya's account of the first nuns and the loss of the Theravada nuns' lineage frame a living debate over women's full ordination.
reading: The Vinaya, in the Cullavagga, tells how Mahapajapati Gotami, the Buddha's aunt and foster mother, asked to be ordained. The Buddha at first refused. Ananda asked whether women could reach awakening. The Buddha, as the text presents him, said yes, and allowed ordination with eight special rules, the *garudhammas*, that placed nuns under monks in certain ways.

The order of fully ordained Theravada nuns, bhikkhunis, died out in Sri Lanka around the eleventh century. The Vinaya requires both monks and nuns for a nun's ordination, so many Theravada authorities hold that the lineage cannot be revived. East Asian traditions kept their nuns' lineage, and in 1996 and 1998 Sri Lankan women were ordained with help from Korean and Taiwanese nuns.

Today the debate continues. Some Theravada monks, such as Ajahn Brahm in Australia in 2009, have supported ordinations and faced sanctions. Some traditional authorities reject them as invalid. Many women practice as ten-precept nuns without full ordination. Tibetan traditions have been discussing full ordination too. Scholars and practitioners read the same Vinaya passages to reach different *conclusions*.

words.d: a fully ordained Buddhist nun
the eight special rules the Vinaya says were given for nuns
the Buddha's aunt and foster mother, the first nun in Vinaya tradition
a judgment reached by reasoning from evidence

lessons.title: Readings for the Earth
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhist environmentalists read texts on interdependence, the precepts and the forest life as grounds for protecting nature.
reading: Beginning in the late 1980s, some Thai monks wrapped trees in orange robes and ordained them, so that cutting them would be seen as harming a monk. Scholars such as Susan Darlington call them *ecology monks*. They drew on the forest settings of the Buddha's life, the precept against taking life, and the respect owed to the robe.

Other readers draw on the texts directly. Dhammapada 49 compares the sage to a bee who takes nectar without harming the flower's color or scent. Thai reformer Sulak Sivaraksa and American writer Joanna Macy read dependent arising as teaching that humans and nature are bound together. Thich Nhat Hanh wrote of the earth as a living mother.

Some scholars caution that early texts were not written with modern ecology in mind. The suttas describe forests as places of practice and sometimes of danger, and rules against harming plants belong to monastic discipline. Environmental Buddhists answer that each generation applies the texts to its own suffering. Both points belong in a careful account of *eco-Buddhism*.

words.d: Thai monks who use Buddhist ritual, such as tree ordination, to protect forests
Buddhist readings and movements that apply teachings to protecting nature
the idea that all things depend on one another; related to dependent arising

lessons.title: Inside and Outside
lessons.mainIdea: Modern readers include monks, lay teachers, reformers, converts and academic scholars, and each brings different aims to the texts.
reading: Who counts as a reader of the Buddhist texts? Monks and nuns who chant them daily. Laypeople who hear them at funerals. Reformers like Ambedkar. Teachers like Thich Nhat Hanh. Scientists in dialogue with the Dalai Lama. And academic scholars, many of whom are not Buddhist, who study the texts historically.

Religious studies scholars sometimes speak of *insider* and *outsider* readers. An insider reads the text as part of their own practice and community. An outsider reads it from a distance, asking historical or comparative questions. Many people are both: a Buddhist scholar, or a non-Buddhist who has practiced for years. The terms describe stances more than people.

Each stance sees things the other can miss. Insiders know how a text lives: what is chanted, when, and why it moves people. Outsiders may notice change over time and parallels in other traditions. This course takes an outsider's descriptive stance while treating insider readings as authoritative for their communities. That is not a ranking. It is a method.

words.d: a reader who approaches a text as part of their own religious practice
a reader who studies a text from outside the practicing community
the position from which a reader approaches a text

lessons.title: Reading Without Ranking
lessons.mainIdea: A careful student can compare modern readings by asking what text each uses, what question it answers and whom it serves, without ranking them.
reading: This chapter has met many modern readings. Ambedkar read the texts for social equality. Thich Nhat Hanh read them for peace and interbeing. The Dalai Lama read them in dialogue with science. Women seeking ordination read the Vinaya for precedent. Ecology monks read them for the earth. Each is a real *interpretation*.

One way to compare without ranking uses three questions. What passages does the reader cite? What question from their own time are they answering? Which community do they speak for and to? These questions turn opinions into evidence. They let a student explain why readers differ instead of simply declaring a winner.

Traditional readers raise a fourth question: does the reading stay faithful to the texts and the lineage? Modern readers often answer that faithfulness means applying the Dhamma to present suffering. That debate itself is part of the tradition. A careful student can report it, weigh the evidence each side gives, and still leave the verdict to the communities themselves.

words.d: a reader's account of what a text means
an earlier case used to guide a later decision
staying true to a text's words or a tradition's teaching
